oneLine: 2 Thessalonians is a short letter to a young group of Jesus followers in the Greek city of Thessalonica, written to calm their confusion about the end of the world and to encourage them to keep living steady, ordinary, faithful lives.
writtenBy: The letter names Paul as its author, writing together with his co-workers Silas (called Silvanus here) and Timothy, and near the end Paul says he is signing it in his own hand. That has been the traditional view for most of history. Many modern scholars, however, think it may have been written later by a follower of Paul using his name, partly because its tone and its picture of the end times differ from 1 Thessalonians. Others still hold that Paul wrote it. Scholars remain divided.
when: If Paul wrote it, it was probably sent around AD 50 or 51, likely from the city of Corinth, a few months after 1 Thessalonians. If a later follower wrote it, the date would be some decades after that. Either way, the readers were a small, mostly non-Jewish community facing hostility from their neighbours for their new faith.
writtenTo: The community of Jesus followers in Thessalonica, a busy port city in Macedonia in northern Greece. Paul had started this group only a short time before.
why: Some in the community had been unsettled by a message, possibly even a letter claiming to be from Paul, saying that 'the day of the Lord' had already arrived. That phrase means the time when Jesus returns and God sets the world right. The letter answers that this day has not yet come, encourages the readers to hold on through suffering, and tells those who had stopped working to get back to normal life. In the Bible's bigger story, it shows early Christians learning to live with hope for the future without letting that hope pull them away from everyday responsibility.
themes: The day of the Lord has not come yet

readingTip: Chapter 2 talks about a 'man of lawlessness' and something that is 'holding him back,' and no one today knows for certain what these meant. Scholars have offered many guesses, so it helps to focus on the letter's clear main point: do not panic, the end has not arrived. Also be aware that chapter 1 speaks bluntly about God punishing those who trouble the readers. It is a hard passage, written to people who were being mistreated, and it is worth reading slowly rather than skipping.
